reason: The run splits the same relational sense between 'fellowship' (2 Cor 6:14; 13:13; 1 John 1:3, 6, 7), 'partnership' with a departure note (1 Cor 1:9) and 'the common life' (Acts 2:42). It also renders the same phrase, κοινωνία of the Spirit, as 'fellowship of the Holy Spirit' in 2 Cor 13:13 but 'sharing in the Spirit' in Phil 2:1. The word has three distinguishable senses (bond between persons, participation in a thing, concrete generosity), and translators choosing chapter by chapter will keep drawing the lines differently unless the register fixes them.
sense: Bond of shared life and close association between persons, whether among believers or between believers and God, Christ or the Spirit. This is the relational sense only; participation in a thing and concrete generosity are covered by alternates.

alternates.when: The word denotes joint engagement in a shared undertaking or working agreement, not the relationship as such: Gal 2:9 (right hand of partnership), Phil 1:5 (partnership in the good news), Phlm 6 (partnership of your faith, linked to 'partner' in v. 17).

The word is followed by a genitive of the thing shared in and the sense is taking part in it: 1 Cor 10:16 (blood and body of Christ), Phil 3:10 (his sufferings), 2 Cor 8:4 (the service to the holy ones). This does not apply to the genitive 'of the Spirit' in 2 Cor 13:13 and Phil 2:1, which take the default 'fellowship of the Spirit' so that the open genitive is kept and the two verses match.
The word denotes concrete generosity, the act of sharing goods or money with others: Rom 15:26, 2 Cor 9:13, Heb 13:16. A verbal recast such as 'to share' is acceptable where English needs it.

traditional: fellowship (also 'communion' in 1 Cor 10:16 and 2 Cor 13:13; 'contribution' in Rom 15:26)
rationale: The Greek word means having something in common, and it covered business partnerships and marriage as well as friendship. For the bond between persons, 'fellowship' is still the English word that best holds both the relationship and the shared life, and a lexicographer would list it. 'Partnership' sounds commercial and implies equals when used of the Father or the Son, so it is kept for the passages where a joint undertaking is in view. A note can warn that the word is stronger than modern 'fellowship' may suggest.
standard_view: Most translations (KJV, NASB, ESV, NIV, NRSV) use 'fellowship' for the relational sense in Acts 2:42, 1 Cor 1:9, 2 Cor 6:14, Gal 2:9 and 1 John 1. They use 'participation', 'sharing' or 'communion' in 1 Cor 10:16 and Phil 3:10, 'contribution' or 'sharing' in Rom 15:26, 2 Cor 9:13 and Heb 13:16, and often 'partnership' in Phil 1:5. They divide over the Spirit phrases: 2 Cor 13:13 is usually 'fellowship' or 'communion of the Holy Spirit', while Phil 2:1 is often 'participation in' or 'sharing in the Spirit', and many scholars favour the participation reading in both. Acts 2:42 is disputed between the community's bond in general and the sharing of goods specifically, and Phlm 6 is widely regarded as obscure. Most versions keep 'fellowship' in Gal 2:9, so 'partnership' there is an editorial departure, though lexically well supported.
